$comment: ClaimDesk 247 — Property Damage (Third-Party Motor) sub-tree (v1). The beachhead product per THIRD-PARTY-MOTOR-CLAIM-FOCUS-2026-07-05.md §3-4 and HOW-TO-WIN-3P-MOTOR-2026-07-05.md. Governing frame: common-law negligence for the liability question + Arsalan v Rixon; Nguyen v Cassim [2021] HCA 274 CLR 606 for the like-for-like hire/recovery question. This is LANE 1 (property damage) — OUTSIDE the NSW Claim Farming Practices Prohibition Act 2025 (which covers personal injury only). No law firm required to run the recovery; referral fees in this lane are lawful and standard. EVERY scenario here is property-damage-only: any injury mention is firewalled to esc-injury → PI pathway, never monetized per-referral. Every rule and threshold is a DRAFT for Legal Head sign-off under CD-E4/CD-G2. Per-tree hashing: this tree's sign-off is bound to its own scenarios[] hash, independent of motor/PL/med-neg. Band enum strictly likely|possible|unclear|insufficient. No numeric fault %.
governing_law: Common law negligence (liability) + Arsalan v Rixon; Nguyen v Cassim [2021] HCA 274 CLR 606 (like-for-like hire/recovery). NOT the Motor Accidents Injuries Act 2012017 (NSW) — that is the CTP injury scheme (Lane 2).
spec_change: v1.0.0 — Initial PD sub-tree. Scenarios pd1-pd7 mirror the motor liability geometry but with recovery-framed outputs (Arsalan/hire entitlement) and PD-specific quantum + recovery escalation overrides. Lane 1 (property damage) — outside claim-farming ban.

global_escalation_triggers.condition: ANY injury mentioned — hard firewall to PI pathway. Never monetized per-referral. This is the red line (Focus Study §6, How-to-Win §8.6).

rule_citations.title: Keeping a safe distance behind vehicles

rule_citations.rule: Arsalan v Rixon; Nguyen v Cassim [2021] HCA 274 CLR 606
rule_citations.title: Not-at-fault owner's entitlement to like-for-like hire including loss of amenity/enjoyment

classification_questions.question_web: In the collision, your vehicle was:
Just before impact, your vehicle was:
How many vehicles were involved altogether?

default_pattern.description: Following driver responsible for safe gap (RR126); not-at-fault front driver recovers repairs + like-for-like hire (Arsalan)

exceptions.probe_question: Did the vehicle in front brake suddenly without apparent reason?
Were the front vehicle's brake lights working?
Did the vehicle in front reverse into you?

damage_consistency_check.expected: rear damage on front vehicle AND front damage on rear vehicle

band_logic.when: user was the front/stopped vehicle, no exceptions, damage consistent

outputs.text_web: In a rear-end collision in NSW, the following driver is responsible for keeping a safe distance (Road Rule 126). Based on what you've described, the other driver appears liable for the damage to your vehicle, which means their insurer should cover your repairs, towing, and a like-for-like replacement vehicle for the period you're without yours (Arsalan v Rixon, High Court of Australia). We can run that recovery for you. {{ATTACH:master}}

Your rear-end matter looks recoverable, but something you've described (such as sudden braking or a brake-light issue) can affect how the liability is assessed. We'll review the details and tell you honestly whether recovery is worth running. {{ATTACH:master}}

The circumstances of your rear-end collision don't fit the standard pattern neatly — the damage locations or sequence raise questions. This is exactly the kind of matter a person should have reviewed properly before accepting the insurer's first offer. {{ATTACH:master}}
There isn't enough detail yet to assess your matter. Tell us a bit more and we'll review it. {{ATTACH:master}}
